claim: HIV-AFMACS is an HIV reporter virus displaying a streptavidin-binding affinity tag at the surface of infected cells.
source: In this study, we develop an HIV reporter virus (HIV-AFMACS) displaying a streptavidin-binding affinity tag at the surface of infected cells, allowing facile one-step selection with streptavidin-conjugated magnetic beads.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the development of HIV-AFMACS with a streptavidin-binding affinity tag at the cell surface.

claim: HIV-AFMACS allows one-step selection with streptavidin-conjugated magnetic beads.
source: In this study, we develop an HIV reporter virus (HIV-AFMACS) displaying a streptavidin-binding affinity tag at the surface of infected cells, allowing facile one-step selection with streptavidin-conjugated magnetic beads.
evidence: The abstract describes the functional capability of HIV-AFMACS for magnetic bead selection.

claim: HIV-AFMACS enables obtaining pure populations of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells for proteomic analysis.
source: We use this system to obtain pure populations of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells for detailed proteomic analysis, and quantitate approximately 9000 proteins across multiple donors on a dynamic background of T cell activation.
evidence: The abstract states the system was used to obtain pure populations for proteomic analysis.

claim: Approximately 9000 proteins were quantitated across multiple donors using HIV-AFMACS.
source: We use this system to obtain pure populations of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells for detailed proteomic analysis, and quantitate approximately 9000 proteins across multiple donors on a dynamic background of T cell activation.
evidence: The abstract provides the specific number of proteins quantitated.

claim: 650 HIV-dependent changes were identified with q < 0.05.
source: Amongst 650 HIV-dependent changes (q < 0.05), we describe novel Vif-dependent targets FMR1 and DPH7, and 192 proteins not identified and/or regulated in T cell lines, such as ARID5A and PTPN22.
evidence: The abstract states the number of HIV-dependent changes with statistical significance.

claim: FMR1 and DPH7 are novel Vif-dependent targets.
source: Amongst 650 HIV-dependent changes (q < 0.05), we describe novel Vif-dependent targets FMR1 and DPH7, and 192 proteins not identified and/or regulated in T cell lines, such as ARID5A and PTPN22.
evidence: The abstract explicitly identifies FMR1 and DPH7 as novel Vif-dependent targets.

claim: 192 proteins were not identified and/or regulated in T cell lines.
source: Amongst 650 HIV-dependent changes (q < 0.05), we describe novel Vif-dependent targets FMR1 and DPH7, and 192 proteins not identified and/or regulated in T cell lines, such as ARID5A and PTPN22.
evidence: The abstract states the number of proteins specific to primary T cells.

claim: ARID5A and PTPN22 are examples of proteins not identified and/or regulated in T cell lines.
source: Amongst 650 HIV-dependent changes (q < 0.05), we describe novel Vif-dependent targets FMR1 and DPH7, and 192 proteins not identified and/or regulated in T cell lines, such as ARID5A and PTPN22.
evidence: The abstract provides specific examples of proteins unique to primary T cells.

claim: Remodelling of the host proteome during viral infection may reflect direct effects of viral proteins.
source: Remodelling of the host proteome during viral infection may reflect direct effects of viral proteins, secondary effects or cytopathicity accompanying viral replication, or host countermeasures such as the interferon (IFN) response.
evidence: The introduction states this as a general principle of viral infection.

claim: Remodelling of the host proteome during viral infection may reflect secondary effects or cytopathicity accompanying viral replication.
source: Remodelling of the host proteome during viral infection may reflect direct effects of viral proteins, secondary effects or cytopathicity accompanying viral replication, or host countermeasures such as the interferon (IFN) response.
evidence: The introduction states this as a general principle of viral infection.

claim: Remodelling of the host proteome during viral infection may reflect host countermeasures such as the interferon response.
source: Remodelling of the host proteome during viral infection may reflect direct effects of viral proteins, secondary effects or cytopathicity accompanying viral replication, or host countermeasures such as the interferon (IFN) response.
evidence: The introduction states this as a general principle of viral infection.

claim: Time-dependent changes in protein levels can differentiate direct viral effects from secondary effects and host countermeasures.
source: By defining time-dependent changes in protein levels in infected cells, and correlating temporal profiles of cellular and viral proteins, we have shown that it is possible to differentiate these phenomena, and identify direct cellular targets of human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) and HIV (Greenwood et al., 2016; Matheson et al., 2015; Weekes et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites previous work demonstrating this capability.

claim: Pure populations of synchronously infected cells must be sampled sequentially for time course analysis.
source: To enable time course analysis and minimise confounding effects from uninfected bystander cells, pure populations of synchronously infected cells must be sampled sequentially as they progress through a single round of viral replication.
evidence: The introduction states this as a methodological requirement.

claim: CEM-T4 cells were previously spinoculated with Env-deficient NL4-3-ΔEnv-EGFP virus at high MOI for HIV proteomic studies.
source: In the case of HIV, we previously satisfied these conditions by spinoculating the highly permissive CEM-T4 lymphoblastoid T cell line (Foley et al., 1965; O'Doherty et al., 2000; Popovic et al., 1984) with Env-deficient NL4-3-ΔEnv-EGFP virus (Zhang et al., 2004) at a high multiplicity of infection (MOI) (Greenwood et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction describes previous methodology with citations.

claim: Cancer cell line models are limited by the extent to which they retain characteristics of primary cells.
source: The utility of cancer cell line models (such as CEM-T4) is, however, limited by the extent to which they retain the characteristics of the primary cells from which they were derived, and cancer-specific and in vitro culture-dependent reprogramming are well described (Gillet et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on limitations of cell line models.

claim: HIV accessory proteins Vif, Nef and Vpu are required for viral replication in primary T cells but not in many T cell lines.
source: For example, the HIV accessory proteins Vif, Nef and Vpu are required for viral replication in primary T cells, but not in many T cell lines (Neil et al., 2008; Rosa et al., 2015; Sheehy et al., 2002; Usami et al., 2015), and HIV is restricted by type I IFN in primary T cells, but not CEM-derived T cells (Goujon et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies demonstrating differences between primary and transformed T cells.

claim: HIV is restricted by type I IFN in primary T cells but not CEM-derived T cells.
source: For example, the HIV accessory proteins Vif, Nef and Vpu are required for viral replication in primary T cells, but not in many T cell lines (Neil et al., 2008; Rosa et al., 2015; Sheehy et al., 2002; Usami et al., 2015), and HIV is restricted by type I IFN in primary T cells, but not CEM-derived T cells (Goujon et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites a study showing differential IFN restriction.

claim: Dysregulation of the cellular proteome at high MOIs may not be indicative of protein changes when a single transcriptionally active provirus is present per cell.
source: In addition, whilst ensuring a high % infection, dysregulation of the cellular proteome at high MOIs may not be indicative of protein changes when a single transcriptionally active provirus is present per cell.
evidence: The introduction discusses limitations of high MOI experiments.

claim: HIV-AFMACS encodes a cell surface streptavidin-binding affinity tag.
source: To this end, we have developed an HIV reporter virus encoding a cell surface streptavidin-binding affinity tag, allowing antibody-free magnetic cell sorting of infected cells (AFMACS) (Matheson et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The introduction describes the key feature of the HIV-AFMACS virus.

claim: HIV-AFMACS allows antibody-free magnetic cell sorting of infected cells.
source: To this end, we have developed an HIV reporter virus encoding a cell surface streptavidin-binding affinity tag, allowing antibody-free magnetic cell sorting of infected cells (AFMACS) (Matheson et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The introduction describes the functional capability of HIV-AFMACS.

claim: HIV-AFMACS bypasses the need for high MOIs or fluorescence-activated cell sorting.
source: This system allows rapid, scalable, affinity purification of HIV-infected cells from mixed cultures, bypassing the need for high MOIs or fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS).
evidence: The introduction states the advantages of the HIV-AFMACS system.

claim: AFMACS-based magnetic selection requires the 38 amino acid streptavidin-binding peptide (SBP) to be displayed at the cell surface.
source: AFMACS-based magnetic selection requires the high-affinity 38 amino acid streptavidin-binding peptide (SBP) (Keefe et al., 2001) to be displayed at the cell surface by fusion to the N-terminus of the truncated Low-affinity Nerve Growth Factor Receptor (SBP-ΔLNGFR) (Ruggieri et al., 1997).
evidence: The Results section describes the molecular requirements for AFMACS with citations.

claim: Cells expressing SBP-ΔLNGFR can be selected directly with streptavidin-conjugated magnetic beads.
source: Cells expressing this marker may be selected directly with streptavidin-conjugated magnetic beads, washed to remove unbound cells, then released by incubation with the naturally occurring vitamin biotin (Matheson et al., 2014).
evidence: The Results section describes the AFMACS procedure with citation.

claim: Selected cells can be released from magnetic beads by incubation with biotin.
source: Cells expressing this marker may be selected directly with streptavidin-conjugated magnetic beads, washed to remove unbound cells, then released by incubation with the naturally occurring vitamin biotin (Matheson et al., 2014).
evidence: The Results section describes the release mechanism with citation.

claim: Three settings for SBP-ΔLNGFR in the proviral construct were considered: fused to Env signal peptide, downstream of nef with P2A peptide, or downstream of nef with IRES.
source: To engineer a single round HIV reporter virus encoding SBP-ΔLNGFR, we considered three settings in the proviral construct: fused to the endogenous Env signal peptide (as a direct replacement for Env); or as an additional cistron, downstream of nef and either a P2A peptide or IRES.
evidence: The Results section describes the design strategy.

claim: Env-deficient pNL4-3-ΔEnv-EGFP (HIV-1) was used as a backbone for HIV-AFMACS construction.
source: We used Env-deficient pNL4-3-ΔEnv-EGFP (HIV-1) as a backbone and, since increased size of lentiviral genome is known to reduce packaging efficiency (Kumar et al., 2001), tested each approach in constructs from which EGFP was removed and/or the 3' long terminal repeat (LTR) truncated.
evidence: The Results section describes the molecular cloning strategy.

claim: Increased size of lentiviral genome reduces packaging efficiency.
source: We used Env-deficient pNL4-3-ΔEnv-EGFP (HIV-1) as a backbone and, since increased size of lentiviral genome is known to reduce packaging efficiency (Kumar et al., 2001), tested each approach in constructs from which EGFP was removed and/or the 3' long terminal repeat (LTR) truncated.
evidence: The Results section cites literature on lentiviral packaging.

claim: All tested viruses expressed SBP-ΔLNGFR at the cell surface of infected cells.
source: As expected, all viruses tested expressed SBP-ΔLNGFR at the cell surface of infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but the larger constructs resulted in lower infectious viral titres (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The Results section describes experimental observations with reference to figure data.

claim: Larger HIV-AFMACS constructs resulted in lower infectious viral titres.
source: As expected, all viruses tested expressed SBP-ΔLNGFR at the cell surface of infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but the larger constructs resulted in lower infectious viral titres (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The Results section describes experimental observations with reference to figure data.

claim: Viruses from selected constructs expressed high levels of SBP-ΔLNGFR 48 hr post-infection.
source: Viruses generated from these constructs expressed high levels of SBP-ΔLNGFR 48 hr post-infection, and depleted CD4 and tetherin to a similar extent.
evidence: The Results section describes experimental observations.

claim: Viruses from selected constructs depleted CD4 and tetherin to a similar extent.
source: Viruses generated from these constructs expressed high levels of SBP-ΔLNGFR 48 hr post-infection, and depleted CD4 and tetherin to a similar extent.
evidence: The Results section describes experimental observations.

claim: Only pNL4-3-ΔENV-Nef-P2A-SBP-ΔLNGFR virus expressed high levels of LNGFR 24 hr post-infection in both CEM-T4s and primary human CD4+ T cells.
source: However, only the pNL4-3-ΔENV-Nef-P2A-SBP-ΔLNGFR virus (Figure 1B) expressed high levels of LNGFR 24 hr post-infection in both CEM-T4s (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and primary human CD4+ T cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: The Results section describes experimental observations with reference to figures.

claim: Nef-P2A-SBP-ΔLNGFR expression from completely spliced transcripts occurs early in HIV infection.
source: This is consistent with Nef-P2A-SBP-ΔLNGFR expression from completely spliced transcripts early in HIV infection (Klotman et al., 1991), with the P2A peptide ensuring that translation of Nef and SBP-ΔLNGFR follow similar kinetics.
evidence: The Results section provides mechanistic explanation with citation.

claim: The P2A peptide ensures that translation of Nef and SBP-ΔLNGFR follow similar kinetics.
source: This is consistent with Nef-P2A-SBP-ΔLNGFR expression from completely spliced transcripts early in HIV infection (Klotman et al., 1991), with the P2A peptide ensuring that translation of Nef and SBP-ΔLNGFR follow similar kinetics.
evidence: The Results section provides mechanistic explanation.

claim: Purities of ≥ 90% were routinely achieved by AFMACS of both CEM-T4s and primary human CD4+ T cells.
source: In fact, from mixed populations containing approximately 20–40% infected cells, purities of ≥ 90% were routinely achieved by AFMACS of both CEM-T4s and primary human CD4+ T cells, with ≤ 10% infected cells lost in the flow-through (Figure 1E).
evidence: The Results section describes AFMACS performance with reference to figure.

claim: ≤ 10% infected cells were lost in the flow-through during AFMACS.
source: In fact, from mixed populations containing approximately 20–40% infected cells, purities of ≥ 90% were routinely achieved by AFMACS of both CEM-T4s and primary human CD4+ T cells, with ≤ 10% infected cells lost in the flow-through (Figure 1E).
evidence: The Results section describes AFMACS performance with reference to figure.

claim: The HIV-AFMACS proviral construct will be made available via the NIH AIDS Reagent Program.
source: The full HIV-AFMACS sequence is available from GenBank (accession: MK435310) and in Supplementary file 1, and the proviral construct will be made available to the community via the National Institutes of Health (NIH) AIDS Reagent Program.
evidence: The Results section states the availability of the construct.

claim: 9070 cellular proteins were quantitated across 10 different conditions in the time course experiment.
source: In total, we quantitated 9070 cellular proteins across 10 different conditions.
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data from the proteomic experiment.

claim: T cell activation caused extensive proteomic remodelling with 2677/9070 (29%) proteins changing by > 2 fold.
source: As previously reported (Geiger et al., 2016), T cell activation itself caused extensive proteomic remodelling, with relative abundances of 2677/9070 (29%) proteins changing by > 2 fold in activated vs resting cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section describes proteomic changes with citation and reference to figure.

claim: Tetherin is upregulated by T cell activation then progressively depleted in HIV-infected cells.
source: For example, the restriction factor tetherin (targeted by HIV-1 Vpu [Neil et al., 2008]) is upregulated by T cell activation, then progressively depleted in HIV-infected (red, SBP-ΔLNGFR positive) but not uninfected (blue, SBP-ΔLNGFR negative) cells (Figure 2C, left panel).
evidence: The Results section describes protein dynamics with citation and reference to figure.

claim: Tetherin is targeted by HIV-1 Vpu.
source: For example, the restriction factor tetherin (targeted by HIV-1 Vpu [Neil et al., 2008]) is upregulated by T cell activation, then progressively depleted in HIV-infected (red, SBP-ΔLNGFR positive) but not uninfected (blue, SBP-ΔLNGFR negative) cells (Figure 2C, left panel).
evidence: The Results section cites literature on Vpu targeting of tetherin.

claim: SAMHD1 is depleted by T cell activation, independent of HIV infection.
source: Conversely, the restriction factor SAMHD1 (targeted by some HIV-2/SIV Vpx and Vpr variants, but not HIV-1 [Hrecka et al., 2011; Laguette et al., 2011; Lim et al., 2012]) is depleted by T cell activation, independent of HIV infection (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: The Results section describes protein dynamics with citations and reference to figure.

claim: SAMHD1 is targeted by some HIV-2/SIV Vpx and Vpr variants, but not HIV-1.
source: Conversely, the restriction factor SAMHD1 (targeted by some HIV-2/SIV Vpx and Vpr variants, but not HIV-1 [Hrecka et al., 2011; Laguette et al., 2011; Lim et al., 2012]) is depleted by T cell activation, independent of HIV infection (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: The Results section cites literature on SAMHD1 targeting.

claim: Levels of many reported Vpu, Nef, Vif and Vpr substrates were reduced by HIV infection in primary T cells.
source: Aside from tetherin, levels of many other reported Vpu (CD4, SNAT1) (Matheson et al., 2015; Willey et al., 1992), Nef (CD4, SERINC5) (Guy et al., 1987; Rosa et al., 2015; Usami et al., 2015), Vif (APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 families) (Greenwood et al., 2016; Sheehy et al., 2002) and Vpr (UNG, HLTF, ZGPAT, VPRBP, MUS81, EME1, MCM10, TET2) (Hrecka et al., 2016; Lahouassa et al., 2016; Lapek et al., 2017; Lv et al., 2018; Maudet et al., 2013; Romani et al., 2015; Schröfelbauer et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2016) substrates were all reduced by HIV infection in primary T cells (Figure 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The Results section describes protein depletion with multiple citations and references to figures.

claim: APOBEC3B and SERINC1 were not depleted by HIV infection.
source: Conversely, and consistent with our previous observations in CEM-T4s, APOBEC3B and SERINC1 were not depleted (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) (Greenwood et al., 2016; Matheson et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section describes proteins not depleted with citations and reference to figure.

claim: Data are consistent with depletion of HLA-A and HLA-B, but not HLA-C.
source: In the absence of donor haplotyping, polymorphisms at the MHC-I locus make routine proteomic quantification problematic. Nonetheless, our data are consistent with depletion of HLA-A and HLA-B, but not HLA-C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), as previously reported for Nef/Vpu variants from NL4-3 HIV (Apps et al., 2016; Cohen et al., 1999; Schwartz et al., 1996).
evidence: The Results section describes HLA depletion patterns with citations and reference to figure.

claim: Gene products from seven viral ORFs were identified.
source: Together with cellular proteins, we identified gene products from seven viral open reading frames (ORFs; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The Results section describes viral protein identification with reference to figure.

claim: Viral regulatory and accessory proteins expressed from fully spliced, Rev-independent transcripts (Tat, Rev, Nef-P2A and SBP-ΔLNGFR) were expressed early in infection, peaking at 24 hr.
source: As expected (Karn and Stoltzfus, 2012), viral regulatory and accessory proteins expressed from fully spliced, Rev-independent transcripts (Tat, Rev, Nef-P2A and SBP-ΔLNGFR) were expressed early in infection, peaking at 24 hr.
evidence: The Results section describes viral protein expression kinetics with citation.

claim: Viral structural proteins expressed from unspliced, Rev-dependent transcripts (Gag and Gagpol) were expressed late in infection, increasing progressively from 24 to 48 hr.
source: Conversely, viral structural proteins expressed from unspliced, Rev-dependent transcripts (Gag and Gagpol) were expressed late in infection, increasing progressively from 24 to 48 hr.
evidence: The Results section describes viral protein expression kinetics.

claim: 8789 cellular proteins were quantitated across nine different conditions in the single time point experiment.
source: In total, we quantitated 8789 cellular proteins across nine different conditions, of which 650 were significantly regulated by HIV infection (q < 0.05) and are summarised in an interactive filter table (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data from the proteomic experiment.

claim: All accessory protein substrates from the time course experiment were significantly depleted by WT HIV in the single time point experiment.
source: Whilst some donor-dependent differences were apparent, most sample-sample variability was accounted for by HIV infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and all accessory protein substrates from Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B were significantly depleted by WT HIV (Figure 3C, left panel).
evidence: The Results section describes reproducibility of findings with reference to figures.

claim: PPP2R5A-E (B56) family of PP2A phosphatase regulatory subunits are degraded by diverse Vif variants, spanning primate and ruminant lentiviruses.
source: Aside from APOBEC3 proteins, we recently discovered the PPP2R5A-E (B56) family of PP2A phosphatase regulatory subunits to be degraded by diverse Vif variants, spanning primate and ruminant lentiviruses (Greenwood et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section cites previous discovery with citation.

claim: Most protein-level changes in HIV-infected CEM-T4s may be explained by primary and secondary effects of Vpr, including degradation of at least 34 additional substrates.
source: As well as 'canonical' accessory protein targets, we have recently discovered that most protein-level changes in HIV-infected CEM-T4s may be explained by primary and secondary effects of Vpr, including degradation of at least 34 additional substrates (Greenwood et al., 2019).
evidence: The Results section cites recent discovery with citation.

claim: Vpr-dependent changes were recapitulated in primary T cells, with 33 newly described Vpr substrates quantitated and 32 decreased in abundance.
source: These changes were recapitulated in primary T cells (Figure 3C, middle panel), with 33 newly described Vpr substrates quantitated, and 32 decreased in abundance.
evidence: The Results section describes validation of Vpr targets with reference to figure.

claim: Known accessory protein-dependent changes are able to account for 297/650 (46%) of proteins regulated by HIV in primary T cells.
source: Nonetheless, taken together, known accessory protein-dependent changes, characterised in transformed T cell lines, are able to account for 297/650 (46%) of proteins regulated by HIV in primary T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), including 175/299 (59%) of proteins decreased in abundance.
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative analysis with reference to figure.

claim: Pathways downregulated by HIV infection of primary T cells include the DNA damage response and cell cycle (Vpr).
source: As with individual proteins, pathways and processes downregulated by HIV infection of primary T cells are dominated by the effects of accessory proteins (Figure 4A–B). These include the DNA damage response and cell cycle (Vpr) (Greenwood et al., 2019; He et al., 1995; Jowett et al., 1995; Laguette et al., 2014; Poon et al., 1997; Re et al., 1995; Rogel et al., 1995; Roshal et al., 2003), cytidine deamination and PP2A activity (Vif) (Greenwood et al., 2016; Harris et al., 2003; Sheehy et al., 2002) and amino acid transport (Vpu/Nef) (Matheson et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section describes pathway analysis with citations and reference to figures.

claim: Pathways downregulated by HIV infection of primary T cells include cytidine deamination and PP2A activity (Vif).
source: As with individual proteins, pathways and processes downregulated by HIV infection of primary T cells are dominated by the effects of accessory proteins (Figure 4A–B). These include the DNA damage response and cell cycle (Vpr) (Greenwood et al., 2019; He et al., 1995; Jowett et al., 1995; Laguette et al., 2014; Poon et al., 1997; Re et al., 1995; Rogel et al., 1995; Roshal et al., 2003), cytidine deamination and PP2A activity (Vif) (Greenwood et al., 2016; Harris et al., 2003; Sheehy et al., 2002) and amino acid transport (Vpu/Nef) (Matheson et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section describes pathway analysis with citations and reference to figures.

claim: Pathways downregulated by HIV infection of primary T cells include amino acid transport (Vpu/Nef).
source: As with individual proteins, pathways and processes downregulated by HIV infection of primary T cells are dominated by the effects of accessory proteins (Figure 4A–B). These include the DNA damage response and cell cycle (Vpr) (Greenwood et al., 2019; He et al., 1995; Jowett et al., 1995; Laguette et al., 2014; Poon et al., 1997; Re et al., 1995; Rogel et al., 1995; Roshal et al., 2003), cytidine deamination and PP2A activity (Vif) (Greenwood et al., 2016; Harris et al., 2003; Sheehy et al., 2002) and amino acid transport (Vpu/Nef) (Matheson et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section describes pathway analysis with citations and reference to figures.

claim: Marked increases in proteins associated with lipid and sterol metabolism were observed in HIV-infected cells.
source: Proteins upregulated by HIV are more diverse, with fewer dominant functional clusters. Nonetheless, we saw marked increases in proteins associated with lipid and sterol metabolism (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The Results section describes upregulated pathways with reference to figures.

claim: A similar effect on lipid and sterol metabolism has been reported in T cell lines at the transcriptional level and attributed to Nef expression.
source: A similar effect has been reported in T cell lines at the transcriptional level, and attributed to the expression of Nef (Shrivastava et al., 2016; van 't Wout et al., 2005).
evidence: The Results section cites literature on lipid metabolism changes.

claim: Several proteins in lipid and sterol metabolism pathways are indirectly regulated by Vpr.
source: Similarly, several proteins in these pathways are indirectly regulated by Vpr (Figure 4C) (Greenwood et al., 2019).
evidence: The Results section describes Vpr regulation with citation and reference to figure.

claim: 1252/8789 (14%) cellular proteins quantitated in primary T cells were not identified in a previous experiment using CEM-T4s.
source: Despite the overall agreement with cell line data, 1252/8789 (14%) cellular proteins quantitated here were not identified in a previous, similar experiment using CEM-T4s (Greenwood et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative comparison with citation.

claim: 192/650 (30%) proteins regulated by HIV in primary T cells were either not detected or not significantly/concordantly regulated in CEM-T4s.
source: Furthermore, having excluded known accessory-protein dependent changes, 192/650 (30%) proteins regulated by HIV in primary T cells were either not detected, or not significantly/concordantly regulated, in CEM-T4s (Figure 3C, right panel and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative comparison with reference to figures.

claim: Expression of SBP-ΔLNGFR as a transgene does not impact the viability, activation or proliferation of primary T cells.
source: We have previously shown that expression of the SBP-ΔLNGFR selectable marker as a transgene does not impact the viability, activation or proliferation of primary T cells (Matheson et al., 2014).
evidence: The Results section cites previous validation with citation.

claim: Amongst 8518 cellular proteins quantitated in the SBP-ΔLNGFR control experiment, only 37/8518 (0.4%) were significantly perturbed by one or both lentivectors (q < 0.05).
source: In fact, amongst 8518 cellular proteins quantitated across nine different conditions, only 37/8518 (0.4%) were significantly perturbed by one or both lentivectors (q < 0.05), and are summarised in an interactive filter table (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data from control experiment.

claim: No Tat-dependent changes in cellular protein levels were identified despite evidence of robust transactivation of the HIV LTR.
source: Interestingly, despite evidence of robust transactivation of the HIV LTR (resulting in high level expression of SBP-ΔLNGFR at the surface of cells transduced with pTat/SBP-ΔLNGFR), no Tat-dependent changes in cellular protein levels were identified (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C, lower panels and Figure 3—figure supplement 4D, bottom panel).
evidence: The Results section describes negative findings with reference to figures.

claim: Amongst 650 proteins significantly regulated by HIV, 576 were quantitated in the SBP-ΔLNGFR control experiment, of which only one protein (MYB) was also significantly regulated by the control lentivectors.
source: Most importantly, amongst the 650 proteins significantly regulated by HIV, 576 were quantitated in the SBP-ΔLNGFR control experiment, of which only one protein (MYB) was also significantly regulated by the control lentivectors (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D, top and middle panels and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative validation with reference to figures.

claim: ARID5A and PTPN22 were readily identified in proteomic datasets from primary T cells (9–14 unique peptides) but not CEM-T4s.
source: To further validate our proteomic data, we focused on two novel HIV targets with commercially available antibodies: ARID5A and PTPN22. These proteins were readily identified in proteomic datasets from primary T cells (9–14 unique peptides) but not CEM-T4s, and consistently depleted across all donors with a fold change > 2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The Results section describes validation targets with reference to figure.

claim: ARID5A and PTPN22 were consistently depleted across all donors with a fold change > 2.
source: To further validate our proteomic data, we focused on two novel HIV targets with commercially available antibodies: ARID5A and PTPN22. These proteins were readily identified in proteomic datasets from primary T cells (9–14 unique peptides) but not CEM-T4s, and consistently depleted across all donors with a fold change > 2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The Results section describes validation results with reference to figure.

claim: Depletion of ARID5A and PTPN22 was confirmed by immunoblot.
source: As expected, depletion was also seen by immunoblot (Figure 3E).
evidence: The Results section describes immunoblot validation with reference to figure.

claim: Substrates of different HIV accessory proteins can be distinguished by their characteristic patterns of temporal regulation.
source: We previously showed that substrates of different HIV accessory proteins could be distinguished by their characteristic patterns of temporal regulation in HIV-infected CEM-T4s (Greenwood et al., 2016), and similar clustering was observed in primary T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The Results section cites previous work and describes similar findings with reference to figure.

claim: Vpr is packaged stoichiometrically in virions.
source: Vpr is packaged stoichiometrically in virions (Cohen et al., 1990; Yu et al., 1990; Yuan et al., 1990) and, since the number of fusogenic HIV particles exceeds the infectious MOI by at least several fold (Thomas et al., 2007), all cells in our time course experiment were necessarily exposed to incoming Vpr.
evidence: The Results section cites literature on Vpr packaging.

claim: The number of fusogenic HIV particles exceeds the infectious MOI by at least several fold.
source: Vpr is packaged stoichiometrically in virions (Cohen et al., 1990; Yu et al., 1990; Yuan et al., 1990) and, since the number of fusogenic HIV particles exceeds the infectious MOI by at least several fold (Thomas et al., 2007), all cells in our time course experiment were necessarily exposed to incoming Vpr.
evidence: The Results section cites literature on HIV particle infectivity.

claim: Depletion of known Vpr substrates was near-maximal by 24 hr in infected cells, with partial depletion also seen in uninfected cells.
source: Accordingly, depletion of known Vpr substrates was near-maximal by 24 hr in infected (red, SBP-ΔLNGFR positive) cells, with partial depletion also seen in uninfected (blue, SBP-ΔLNGFR negative) cells (Figure 2E, upper panel).
evidence: The Results section describes temporal patterns with reference to figure.

claim: Depletion of known Vif, Nef and Vpu substrates increased progressively from 24 to 48 hr and was only seen in HIV-infected cells.
source: In contrast, since de novo viral protein synthesis is absolutely required, depletion of known Vif, Nef and Vpu substrates increased progressively from 24 to 48 hr, and was only seen in HIV-infected (red, SBP-ΔLNGFR positive) cells (Figure 2E, lower panel).
evidence: The Results section describes temporal patterns with reference to figure.

claim: Based on their patterns of temporal regulation, ARID5A and PTPN22 are very likely to represent novel Vpr substrates, specific for primary T cells.
source: Based on their patterns of temporal regulation, ARID5A and PTPN22 are therefore very likely to represent novel Vpr substrates, specific for primary T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The Results section provides inference based on temporal patterns with reference to figure.

claim: ARID5B is a widely conserved target of Vpr variants from primate lentiviruses.
source: Consistent with this, another member of the ARID5 subfamily of AT-rich interaction domain (ARID)-containing proteins, ARID5B, is a widely conserved target of Vpr variants from primate lentivuses (Greenwood et al., 2019), and shares a similar temporal profile (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The Results section cites recent discovery with reference to figure.

claim: Both APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family proteins were depleted in primary CD4+ T cells infected with WT, but not ΔVif viruses.
source: As predicted, both APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family proteins were depleted in primary CD4+ T cells infected with WT, but not ΔVif viruses (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The Results section describes experimental validation with reference to figures.

claim: Vif-dependent depletion of PPP2R5A-E causes a marked increase in protein phosphorylation in HIV-infected CEM-T4 T cells, particularly substrates of the aurora kinases (AURKA/B).
source: Vif-dependent depletion of PPP2R5A-E causes a marked increase in protein phosphorylation in HIV-infected CEM-T4 T cells, particularly substrates of the aurora kinases (AURKA/B) (Greenwood et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section cites previous findings.

claim: AURKB activity is enhanced by 'activation loop' auto-phosphorylation at threonine 232 (T232), antagonised by PP2A-B56.
source: AURKB activity is enhanced by 'activation loop' auto-phosphorylation at threonine 232 (T232), antagonised by PP2A-B56 (Meppelink et al., 2015; Yasui et al., 2004).
evidence: The Results section cites literature on AURKB regulation.

claim: A marked increase in AURKB T232 phosphorylation is seen in CEM-T4s transduced with Vif as a single transgene.
source: Accordingly, a marked increase in AURKB T232 phosphorylation is seen in CEM-T4s transduced with Vif as a single transgene (Figure 5C).
evidence: The Results section describes experimental observation with reference to figure.

claim: Depletion of PPP2R5D was confirmed by immunoblot of AFMACS-selected primary T cells.
source: We therefore confirmed depletion of PPP2R5D by immunoblot of AFMACS-selected primary T cells and, as a functional correlate, observed increased AURKB phosphorylation (Figure 5D).
evidence: The Results section describes validation with reference to figure.

claim: Increased AURKB phosphorylation was observed as a functional correlate of PPP2R5D depletion in primary T cells.
source: We therefore confirmed depletion of PPP2R5D by immunoblot of AFMACS-selected primary T cells and, as a functional correlate, observed increased AURKB phosphorylation (Figure 5D).
evidence: The Results section describes functional validation with reference to figure.

claim: DPH7 and FMR1 are not known to interact physically with PP2A.
source: Conversely, DPH7 and FMR1 are not known to interact physically with PP2A, and show more profound and consistent depletion (Figure 5E).
evidence: The Results section describes protein characteristics with reference to figure.

claim: DPH7 and FMR1 show more profound and consistent depletion than PP2A-related proteins.
source: Conversely, DPH7 and FMR1 are not known to interact physically with PP2A, and show more profound and consistent depletion (Figure 5E).
evidence: The Results section describes experimental observations with reference to figure.

claim: DPH7 and FMR1 are expressed in CEM-T4 as well as primary T cells and only decreased in abundance in HIV-infected cells in the presence of Vif.
source: To confirm these findings, we first re-examined our proteomic data from CEM-T4s (Greenwood et al., 2016). Unlike ARID5A and PTPN22, DPH7 and FMR1 are expressed in CEM-T4 as well as primary T cells, and only decreased in abundance in HIV-infected cells in the presence of Vif (Figure 5E).
evidence: The Results section describes validation in CEM-T4s with citation and reference to figure.

claim: Vif-dependent depletion of DPH7 and FMR1 was confirmed by immunoblot in cells infected with WT (but not ΔVif) viruses.
source: Next, we confirmed Vif-dependent depletion of both proteins by immunoblot, in cells infected with WT (but not ΔVif) viruses (Figure 5F).
evidence: The Results section describes immunoblot validation with reference to figure.

claim: Vif-dependent depletion of DPH7 and FMR1 was confirmed in cells transduced with Vif as a single transgene.
source: Finally, we repeated these observations in cells transduced with Vif as a single transgene (Figure 5G).
evidence: The Results section describes validation with reference to figure.

claim: Vif is both necessary and sufficient for depletion of DPH7 and FMR1.
source: Vif is therefore both necessary and sufficient for depletion of DPH7 and FMR1 and, taken together with APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family proteins/interactors, we can account for all significant Vif-dependent changes in the natural target cell of HIV infection.
evidence: The Results section provides conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family proteins/interactors together with DPH7 and FMR1 can account for all significant Vif-dependent changes in the natural target cell of HIV infection.
source: Vif is therefore both necessary and sufficient for depletion of DPH7 and FMR1 and, taken together with APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family proteins/interactors, we can account for all significant Vif-dependent changes in the natural target cell of HIV infection.
evidence: The Results section provides comprehensive conclusion.

claim: Bead-based magnetic sorting is fast, simple and scalable compared with FACS.
source: Compared with FACS, bead-based magnetic sorting is fast, simple and scalable for simultaneous processing of multiple samples and large cell numbers (Plouffe et al., 2015).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on advantages of magnetic sorting.

claim: In conventional antibody-based immunomagnetic selection, cells remain coated with beads and antibody-antigen complexes, risking alteration of their behaviour or viability.
source: In conventional, antibody-based immunomagnetic selection, cells remain coated with beads and antibody-antigen complexes, risking alteration of their behaviour or viability through cross-linking of cell-surface receptors or internalisation of ferrous beads (Bernard et al., 2002; Plouffe et al., 2015; Stanciu et al., 1996).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on limitations of conventional magnetic sorting.

claim: AFMACS-based selection is antibody free and selected cells are released from the beads by incubation with biotin.
source: Conversely, AFMACS-based selection is antibody free, and selected cells are released from the beads by incubation with biotin, suitable for a full range of downstream applications (Matheson et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion cites previous work on AFMACS advantages.

claim: The study generated the first high coverage proteomic atlas of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells.
source: To demonstrate the utility of this system and provide a resource for the community, we have generated the first high coverage proteomic atlas of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells.
evidence: The Discussion states the novelty of the resource.

claim: Primary T cells express a full range of proteins relevant to HIV infection in vivo, unlike T cell lines.
source: Unlike T cell lines, primary T cells express a full range of proteins relevant to HIV infection in vivo, and are not confounded by the genetic and epigenetic effects of transformation.
evidence: The Discussion states advantages of primary cells.

claim: Proteins unique to primary T cells were significantly more likely to be regulated by HIV infection than proteins detected in both primary T cells and CEM-T4s (131/1252 = 10.5% vs 519/7537 = 6.9%; p < 0.0001).
source: Furthermore, proteins unique to primary T cells were significantly more likely to be regulated by HIV infection than proteins detected in both primary T cells and CEM-T4s (131/1252 = 10.5% vs 519/7537 = 6.9%; p < 0.0001, two-tailed Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The Discussion provides statistical analysis of protein regulation.

claim: For some Vpu/Nef substrates, downregulation from the plasma membrane may occur in the absence of protein degradation.
source: For some Vpu/Nef substrates, such as NTB-A and CCR7, downregulation from the plasma membrane may occur in the absence of protein degradation (Bolduan et al., 2013; Ramirez et al., 2014; Shah et al., 2010).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on mechanisms of protein regulation.

claim: For some accessory protein targets, expression may prevent upregulation without reducing levels below baseline.
source: For others, such as ICAM-1/3, accessory protein expression may prevent upregulation, without reducing levels below baseline (Sugden et al., 2017).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on mechanisms of protein regulation.

claim: Previous temporal proteomic analyses of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells were hampered by extremely limited coverage of the cellular proteome (< 2000 proteins).
source: Previous temporal proteomic analyses of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells were hampered by extremely limited coverage of the cellular proteome (< 2000 proteins), and did not detect regulation of known or novel HIV accessory protein targets (Chan et al., 2009; Nemeth et al., 2017).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on limitations of previous studies.

claim: A recent study quantitated 7761 proteins in FACS-sorted T cells at 96 hr post-infection with an R5-tropic, GFP-expressing Nef-deficient virus.
source: A more recent study quantitated 7761 proteins in FACS-sorted T cells at a single time point 96 hr post-infection with an R5-tropic, GFP-expressing Nef-deficient virus (Kuo et al., 2018).
evidence: The Discussion cites a recent comparable study.

claim: 413/650 (64%) of the HIV-dependent changes identified in this study were obscured in the Kuo et al. 2018 study.
source: Conversely, the full dataset is not available, effect sizes were generally compressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A), and 413/650 (64%) of the HIV-dependent changes identified in our study were obscured, including depletion of ARID5A, PTPN22, DPH7 and 19/51 known accessory protein substrates (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: The Discussion provides quantitative comparison with reference to figures.

claim: The depth of proteomic coverage in this study reduces the variability in quantitation ('noise').
source: Compared with other studies, the depth of proteomic coverage reported here not only increases the number of proteins identified, but also reduces the variability in quantitation ('noise').
evidence: The Discussion states advantages of the methodology.

claim: > 90% of proteins are quantitated using two or more unique peptides.
source: For example, > 90% of proteins are quantitated using two or more unique peptides.
evidence: The Discussion provides quantitative metric of data quality.

claim: The homogeneous populations of cells analysed (> 90% infected) maximise effect sizes ('signal').
source: Furthermore, the homogeneous populations of cells analysed (> 90% infected) maximise effect sizes ('signal'), and ensure that proteins exhibiting the most statistically significant differences are also those with the biggest fold changes.
evidence: The Discussion explains advantages of high purity cell populations.

claim: The 'signal-to-noise ratio' is high, allowing positive controls (known viral targets) to behave extremely consistently across datasets.
source: Because the 'signal-to-noise ratio' is high, positive controls (known viral targets) behave extremely consistently across our datasets (as shown, for example, in Figure 3C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and it is possible to make predictions about other cellular proteins falling in the same regions of the volcano plots, and/or exhibiting similar temporal profiles.
evidence: The Discussion explains data quality with reference to figures.

claim: Env-deficient proviral backbone and VSVg pseudotyping were used to enhance viral titers, avoid Env-dependent cytotoxicity, enable synchronous single round infections and bypass co-receptor-dependent targeting.
source: To enhance viral titers, avoid Env-dependent cytotoxicity, enable synchronous single round infections and bypass co-receptor-dependent targeting of T cell lineages with pre-existing proteomic differences, we used an Env-deficient proviral backbone and pseudotyped viruses with VSVg.
evidence: The Discussion explains methodological choices.

claim: Pseudotyping with VSVg redirects HIV viral entry away from the plasma membrane towards an endocytic pathway.
source: Pseudotyping with VSVg redirects HIV viral entry away from the plasma membrane towards an endocytic pathway (Aiken, 1997), and may abrogate Env-dependent integrin (Arthos et al., 2008) and chemokine co-receptor (Wu and Yoder, 2009) signalling early in infection.
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on VSVg pseudotyping effects.

claim: Only 1/650 HIV-dependent perturbations was also observed in cells transduced with control lentiviral particles.
source: Since only 1/650 HIV-dependent perturbations at this time point was also observed in cells transduced with control lentiviral particles, it is very unlikely that pseudotyping with VSVg per se caused significant artefactual proteomic changes in our datasets (false positives).
evidence: The Discussion provides quantitative assessment of potential artifacts.

claim: The absence of Env-CD4/co-receptor interactions may have resulted in an underestimate of proteomic changes induced by full length HIV (false negatives).
source: Nonetheless, it is possible that the absence of Env-CD4/co-receptor interactions resulted in an underestimate of proteomic changes induced by full length HIV (false negatives), which may vary depending on tropism of the virus (Wiredja et al., 2018; Wojcechowskyj et al., 2013).
evidence: The Discussion acknowledges potential limitations with citations.

claim: Temporal profiling is particularly well suited to identifying and characterising host factors regulated directly by viral proteins.
source: Temporal profiling is particularly well suited to identifying and characterising host factors regulated directly by viral proteins.
evidence: The Discussion states advantages of temporal profiling.

claim: Accessory proteins account for much or most of the proteomic remodelling in HIV-infected cells.
source: In fact, as we show here, accessory proteins account for much or most of the proteomic remodelling in HIV-infected cells.
evidence: The Discussion provides summary conclusion.

claim: The abundance of direct accessory protein targets likely explains why proteins and processes/pathways downregulated by HIV in primary T cells correlate so well with changes seen in T cell lines.
source: The abundance of direct accessory protein targets likely explains why proteins and processes/pathways downregulated by HIV in primary T cells correlate so well with changes seen in T cell lines, and are robust to inter-individual variation.
evidence: The Discussion provides mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Upregulated proteins concord less well with changes in T cell lines and functional effects are less homogeneous.
source: In comparison, upregulated proteins concord less well with changes in T cell lines, and functional effects are less homogeneous.
evidence: The Discussion provides comparative analysis.

claim: Upregulated proteins may reflect indirect effects (e.g., secondary changes in transcription), which are more likely to be cell-type specific.
source: This may be because upregulated proteins reflect indirect effects (for example, secondary changes in transcription), which are more likely to be cell-type specific.
evidence: The Discussion provides mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Vif was thought until recently to exclusively degrade APOBEC3 family cytidine deaminases.
source: Amongst the HIV accessory proteins, Vif was thought until recently to exclusively degrade APOBEC3 family cytidine deaminases.
evidence: The Discussion states previous understanding.

claim: FMR1 is known to reduce HIV virus infectivity when over-expressed in producer cells.
source: Nonetheless, FMR1 is already known to reduce HIV virus infectivity when over-expressed in producer cells (Pan et al., 2009), and the other novel targets highlighted in this study also impact processes relevant for HIV replication, such as inflammatory cytokine signalling (ARID5A) (Higa et al., 2018), T cell activation (PTPN22) (Hasegawa et al., 2004) and translational fidelity (DPH7) (Carette et al., 2009; Ortiz et al., 2006).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on FMR1 function.

claim: ARID5A impacts inflammatory cytokine signalling.
source: Nonetheless, FMR1 is already known to reduce HIV virus infectivity when over-expressed in producer cells (Pan et al., 2009), and the other novel targets highlighted in this study also impact processes relevant for HIV replication, such as inflammatory cytokine signalling (ARID5A) (Higa et al., 2018), T cell activation (PTPN22) (Hasegawa et al., 2004) and translational fidelity (DPH7) (Carette et al., 2009; Ortiz et al., 2006).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on ARID5A function.

claim: PTPN22 impacts T cell activation.
source: Nonetheless, FMR1 is already known to reduce HIV virus infectivity when over-expressed in producer cells (Pan et al., 2009), and the other novel targets highlighted in this study also impact processes relevant for HIV replication, such as inflammatory cytokine signalling (ARID5A) (Higa et al., 2018), T cell activation (PTPN22) (Hasegawa et al., 2004) and translational fidelity (DPH7) (Carette et al., 2009; Ortiz et al., 2006).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on PTPN22 function.

claim: DPH7 impacts translational fidelity.
source: Nonetheless, FMR1 is already known to reduce HIV virus infectivity when over-expressed in producer cells (Pan et al., 2009), and the other novel targets highlighted in this study also impact processes relevant for HIV replication, such as inflammatory cytokine signalling (ARID5A) (Higa et al., 2018), T cell activation (PTPN22) (Hasegawa et al., 2004) and translational fidelity (DPH7) (Carette et al., 2009; Ortiz et al., 2006).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on DPH7 function.

claim: The diversity of Vif targets underscores the benefit of an unbiased, systems-level approach to viral infection.
source: The diversity of these targets underscores the benefit of an unbiased, systems-level approach to viral infection, and the capacity of the resources presented in this study to reveal unsuspected aspects of the host-virus interaction in the natural target cell of HIV infection.
evidence: The Discussion provides concluding statement.
